label: 0–6 weeks (newborn)
blurb: Very new. Short, local trips only — we'll show you what's safe.
title: 0–6 weeks: Start small, and that's more than fine.
body: These first weeks are for getting to know each other, so there's no rush. If you do need to fly, the American Academy of Pediatrics says it's generally safe once a healthy baby is at least 7 days old, but suggests waiting until 2–3 months if you can.
points: Short car journeys are a gentle way to start. The Lullaby Trust suggests avoiding long drives with very young babies, and stopping for regular breaks
A night or two somewhere nearby makes a lovely practice trip
Get comfortable with your baby kit first. Everything else can wait
flightNote: Each airline sets its own minimum age. British Airways accepts babies from 48 hours old but recommends waiting a week; easyJet's minimum is 14 days. If your baby was born early or had any complications, check with your GP and the airline first, as some ask for medical clearance.

label: 6 weeks – 3 months
blurb: Immune system strengthening. A great window for short flights.
title: 6 weeks – 3 months: A lovely time for a first short trip.
body: Healthy babies this age can usually fly, and because they're not on the move yet, journeys can be simpler than you'd expect. If your baby was born early or has a health condition, have a quick chat with your GP or health visitor first.
points: Lots of sleep at this age can make long journeys calmer than you'd think
Not crawling yet, so keeping them safe and settled is simpler
Feeding or a dummy during take-off and landing can help with ear pressure

label: 3 – 6 months
blurb: Often called the travel "sweet spot." Alert but not yet mobile.
title: 3–6 months: The travel sweet spot. Seriously.
body: Many parents call this the easiest window to travel. Babies are alert and engaging but not yet crawling or walking. They sleep in carriers and strollers. They're charmed by new faces.
points: Long-haul flights: ask about a bassinet when you book. They're limited, and each airline has its own limits (British Airways' carrycots are for babies up to 6 months and 8kg)
Restaurant dinners (they'll be entertained by the environment)
Naps in a carrier or stroller let you keep exploring

label: 6 – 12 months
blurb: More interactive, with more opinions. Can still travel on your lap.
title: 6–12 months: Wonderful — with a bit more planning.
body: Babies at this age are interactive, curious, and developing strong opinions about what they want. This is wonderful — and means you'll want more activities and more snacks.
points: Babies can travel on your lap until their 2nd birthday. If they turn 2 during the trip, they'll need their own seat from then on
Solid foods mean you can buy food locally — lighter packing
Crawling babies need safe spaces — check hotel room carefully

label: 12 – 18 months
blurb: Walking + curious = plan for exploration time at every stop.
title: 12–18 months: They want to walk. Let them.
body: New walkers are explorers. Build walking time into every stop — airports, parks, hotel corridors. A toddler who's moved their body is a toddler who sleeps.
points: Choose destinations with parks, beaches, or open walking space
Schedule activities in the morning alert window
Carry a carrier as backup when legs give out suddenly

label: 18 months – 2 years
blurb: Strong opinions and big personality. Still very manageable with prep.
title: 18 months – 2 years: Big personality, big fun.
body: Toddlers at this age have preferences, language emerging, and strong feelings about things. That's also what makes travel with them memorable.
points: Give them "choices" within your plan ("Do you want to go to the park or the beach first?")
Keep snacks visible and accessible at all times
Download 2–3 favourite shows for transit — no guilt
